and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is

e-4833.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consists of the vectors $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2,$ and $\mathbf e_3,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/0d9a23830f48d4659dd963110d9322c12e8d4849bd9bcd63ae9d5adb0e1fba05.png)

The components of the vectors in $\mathcal{B}$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

e-4835.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
e-4835.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/07a8e394234737d51a0064816b255569d20e826eb3a82884a24f1fc0a9fa6baa.png)
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$
e-4835.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} & -3 \\ \frac{3}{2} & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-4837.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
e-4837.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/51b47f81b941fffa62d1f8402a4ef08b9b7d1636b1a37a86578311f1db192b3d.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/a9964c0672c8859f4b4857d422e25a435ed0be907c074a22b7cc12729f051613.png) be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$
e-4837.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065461/assets/60eb4bbd057feab1b78fb283e951dc8c35f9a95875bd46f078c87c25b3b749c8.png)

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 22 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}\,4 & 22 \\ \,1 & 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ If ${b}_{1}=5{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ from $B$ to $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].

Question 1
?

Let B={b1,b2} and C={c1,c2} be bases of R2. If b1=5c2−3c1 and b2=2c1−4c2, find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C from B to C.

a
[−345−2]
b
[5−4−32]
c
[−325−4]
d
[−523−4]
e
[−352−4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in B relative to the basis C are [b1]C=[−35][b2]C=[2−4].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain PB→C=[−325−4].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
content.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ If ${b}_{1}=5{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}=2{c}_{1}-4{c}_{2},$ find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ from $B$ to $C.$
content.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

Let B={b1,b2} and C={c1,c2} be bases of R2. If b1=2c1−7c2 and b2=4c2−3c1, find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C from B to C.

a
[42−7−3]
b
[24−7−3]
c
[42−3−7]
d
[−324−7]
e
[2−3−74]
Submit

decision.explanation: The columns of P_{B→C} are the C-coordinates of b₁ and b₂. From b₁ = 2c₁ − 7c₂ and b₂ = −3c₁ + 4c₂, these columns are (2, −7) and (−3, 4), respectively.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ If ${b}_{1}=2{c}_{1}-7{c}_{2}$ and ${b}_{2}=4{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1},$ find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ from $B$ to $C.$
after.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

before.name: Question 3
before.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =3{b}_{3}-{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4{b}_{2}-5{b}_{1}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2{b}_{1}+3{b}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is

$$

Question 3
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

c1=3b3−b1+b2,c2=4b2−5b1,c3=2b1+3b3,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is

PC→B=[a−521b030c]?

a
a=1, b=−5, and c=2
b
a=3, b=0, and c=3
c
a=3, b=4, and c=0
d
a=−1, b=0, and c=0
e
a=−1, b=4, and c=3
Submit

decision.explanation: The columns are the B-coordinates of c₁, c₂, and c₃: (−1,1,3), (−5,4,0), and (2,0,3). Comparing entries gives a = −1, b = 4, and c = 3.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =3{b}_{3}-{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4{b}_{2}-5{b}_{1}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2{b}_{1}+3{b}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & c\end{aligned}]?
$$
after.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $C$ relative to the basis $B$ are

$$
[{c}_{1}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{2}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{3}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-1,$ $b=4,$ and $c=3.$

after.html:
Question 3
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

c1=3b3−b1+b2,c2=4b2−5b1,c3=2b1+3b3,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is

PC→B=[a−521b030c]?

a
a=1, b=−5, and c=2
b
a=3, b=0, and c=3
c
a=3, b=4, and c=0
d
a=−1, b=0, and c=0
e
a=−1, b=4, and c=3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in C relative to the basis B are

[c1]B=[−113],[c2]B=[−540],[c3]B=[203].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of C relative to the basis B.

Therefore, we obtain

PC→B=[−1−52140303].

Finally, a=−1, b=4, and c=3.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =3{b}_{3}-{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4{b}_{2}-5{b}_{1}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2{b}_{1}+3{b}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & c\end{aligned}]?
$$
content.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $C$ relative to the basis $B$ are

$$
[{c}_{1}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{2}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{3}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-1,$ $b=4,$ and $c=3.$

before.name: Question 4
before.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B$ given that

$$
[{c}_{1}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{2}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B$ given that

$$
[{c}_{1}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,[{c}_{2}]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}-{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =5{c}_{3}+2{c}_{2}, \\ {b}_{3} & ={c}_{2}-{c}_{1},\end{aligned}

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ a & b & 1 \\ -1 & c & 0\end{aligned}]?

before.html:
Question 5
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=c1+2c2−c3,b2=5c3+2c2,b3=c2−c1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is

PB→C=[10−1ab1−1c0]?

a
a=1, b=−2, and c=5
b
a=2, b=0, and c=−1
c
a=0, b=2, and c=−1
d
a=1, b=2, and c=0
e
a=2, b=2, and c=5
Submit

decision.explanation: The columns are the C-coordinates of b₁, b₂, and b₃: (1,2,−1), (0,2,5), and (−1,1,0). Comparing entries gives a = 2, b = 2, and c = 5.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}-{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =5{c}_{3}+2{c}_{2}, \\ {b}_{3} & ={c}_{2}-{c}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ a & b & 1 \\ -1 & c & 0\end{aligned}]?
$$
after.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=c1+2c2−c3,b2=5c3+2c2,b3=c2−c1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is

PB→C=[10−1ab1−1c0]?

a
a=1, b=−2, and c=5
b
a=2, b=0, and c=−1
c
a=0, b=2, and c=−1
d
a=1, b=2, and c=0
e
a=2, b=2, and c=5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in B relative to the basis C are

[b1]C=[12−1],[b2]C=[025],[b3]C=[−110].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain

PB→C=[10−1221−150].

Finally, a=2, b=2, and c=5.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}-{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =5{c}_{3}+2{c}_{2}, \\ {b}_{3} & ={c}_{2}-{c}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ a & b & 1 \\ -1 & c & 0\end{aligned}]?
$$
content.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Let B={b1,b2} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→S from B to S if b1=[1−2],b2=[1−3].

a
[11−2−3]
b
[−3121]
c
[−211−3]
d
[−2−311]
e
[11−3−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1 and e2, given by e1=[10],e2=[01].

The components of the vectors of B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[1−2],[b2]S=[1−3]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[11−2−3].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 7
?

Let B={b1,b2} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→S from B to S if b1=[−2−3],b2=[7−4].

a
[7−2−4−3]
b
[−27−3−4]
c
[−47−3−2]
d
[−2−37−4]
e
[2−734]
Submit

decision.explanation: The columns of P_{B→S} are the given standard coordinates of b₁ and b₂, in order: (−2, −3) and (7, −4). This gives option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

after.html:
Question 8
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} be a basis of R3 and let S be the standard basis of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=[−340],b2=[−5−10],b3=[001],

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[a−504b000c].

a
a=0, b=0, and c=1
b
a=−3, b=0, and c=0
c
a=−3, b=0, and c=4
d
a=−5, b=4, and c=1
e
a=−3, b=−1, and c=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R3 consists of the vectors e1,e2, and e3, given by e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001].

The components of the vectors in B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[−340],[b2]S=[−5−10],[b3]S=[001]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[−3−504−10001].

Finally, a=−3, b=−1, and c=1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & a & -3 \\ b & -2 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 & c\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=7,$ $b=0,$ and $c=0.$

Let B={b1,b2,b3} be a basis of R3 and let S be the standard basis of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=[10−1],b2=[7−23],b3=[−340],

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[1a−3b−24−13c].

a
a=7, b=0, and c=0
b
a=0, b=7, and c=0
c
a=1, b=−2, and c=0
d
a=0, b=3, and c=−3
e
a=7, b=0, and c=−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R3 consists of the vectors e1,e2, and e3, given by e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001].

The components of the vectors in B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[10−1],[b2]S=[7−23],[b3]S=[−340]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[17−30−24−130].

Finally, a=7, b=0, and c=0.

verification.explanation: Using the given vectors as columns gives a = 7 (first component of b₂), b = 0 (second component of b₁), and c = 0 (third component of b₃). This matches the revealed worked solution and option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & a & -3 \\ b & -2 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 & c\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=7,$ $b=0,$ and $c=0.$

after.problem:

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].

after.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 10
?

Let B={b1,b2} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→S from B to S if b1=[21],b2=[1−1].

a
[211−1]
b
[111−2]
c
[21−11]
d
[211−2]
e
[121−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1 and e2, given by e1=[10],e2=[01].

The components of the vectors of B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[21],[b2]S=[1−1]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[211−1].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
content.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].$
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].$
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
content.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis C to the basis B is given by PC→B=[57−3−4]. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C .

a
[−4−735]
b
[−43−75]
c
[53−7−4]
d
[−473−5]
e
[3−547]
Submit

decision.explanation: The reverse change-of-coordinates matrix is the inverse. The determinant is 5(−4) − 7(−3) = 1, so the inverse has rows (−4, −7) and (3, 5), giving option a.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-4)-7\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-4)-7\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

history.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-4)-7\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-3)-2\cdot (-9)}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 3 & \frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis C to the basis B is given by PC→B=[52−9−3]. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C .

a
[53−233−1]
b
[5323−3−1]
c
[13−23−53]
d
[−1−23353]
e
[−123−353]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of PC→B, we get

PB→C=PC→B−1=[52−9−3]−1=15⋅(−3)−2⋅(−9)[−3−295]=13⋅[−3−295]=[−1−23353].

verification.explanation: The reverse matrix is the inverse. The determinant is 5(−3) − 2(−9) = 3, giving inverse rows (−1, −2/3) and (3, 5/3). This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
content.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-3)-2\cdot (-9)}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 3 & \frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}].$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 7-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis B to the basis C is given by PB→C=[2357]. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B .

a
[−735−2]
b
[−753−2]
c
[7−3−52]
d
[−235−7]
e
[−253−7]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of PB→C, we get

PC→B=PB→C−1=[2357]−1=12⋅7−3⋅5[7−3−52]=(−1)⋅[7−3−52]=[−735−2].

content.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}].$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
content.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 7-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
after.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

PB→C=PC→B−1=[7394]−1=17⋅4−3⋅9[4−3−97]=1⋅[4−3−97]=[4−3−97].

content.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
content.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
content.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Let B={[63],[−30]} and C={[12],[03]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[2−3−36]
b
[1332]
c
[630−2]
d
[6−3−32]
e
[6331]
Submit

decision.explanation: Since 6c₁ − 3c₂ = (6,3) = b₁ and −3c₁ + 2c₂ = (−3,0) = b₂, their C-coordinate columns are (6,−3) and (−3,2). Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 & 4 \\ -3 & -8 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 17

Let B={[−23],[4−9]} and C={[1−3],[3−8]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[753−3]
b
[−573−3]
c
[7−5−33]
d
[7−3−53]
e
[3−5−37]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: M=[13−24−3−83−9]R2:=R2+3R1∼[13−2401−33]R1:=R1+(−3)R2∼[107−501−33]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[7−5−33].

verification.explanation: Since b₁ = 7c₁ − 3c₂ and b₂ = −5c₁ + 3c₂, their C-coordinate columns are (7,−3) and (−5,3). This confirms option c and matches the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
content.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 & 4 \\ -3 & -8 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $S$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 19

Let B={[12],[11]} be a basis of R2 and S is the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B.

a
[−112−1]
b
[2111]
c
[31−1−12]
d
[1112−1]
e
[121−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and S as {b1,b2} and {e1,e2}, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1=[10],e2=[01].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: M=[11102101]R2:=R2+(−2)R1∼[11100−1−21]R2:=(−1)R2∼[1110012−1]R1:=R1+(−1)R2∼[10−11012−1]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[−112−1].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
content.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $S$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: The matrix from S to B is the inverse of the matrix with columns (17,4) and (4,1). Its determinant is 17·1 − 4·4 = 1, so its inverse has rows (1,−4) and (−4,17), giving option b.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}17 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{17}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{17} & -\frac{4}{17} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=17{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{4}{17} & \frac{1}{17} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 17\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-\frac{4}{17}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 17\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[174104101]R1:=117R1∼[141711704101]R2:=R2+(−4)R1∼[141711700117−4171]R2:=17R2∼[1417117001−417]R1:=R1+(−417)R2∼[101−401−417]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[1−4−417].
